clinicalPearls: An astrocytopathy driven by antibodies to the aquaporin-4 water channel, distinct from multiple sclerosis in both mechanism and treatment.
The clinical hallmarks are severe optic neuritis (often bilateral or sequential) and longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis spanning three or more vertebral segments.
Area postrema syndrome — intractable hiccups, nausea and vomiting from a dorsal medullary lesion — is a highly characteristic presenting feature.
Attacks tend to be far more disabling than in multiple sclerosis and recovery is frequently incomplete, so aggressive acute and preventive treatment is essential.
Serum AQP4-IgG testing by cell-based assay is the key diagnostic test; a seronegative subset exists and some of these patients carry MOG antibodies instead.
Multiple sclerosis disease-modifying agents such as interferon-beta, natalizumab and fingolimod can worsen the disorder and must be avoided.

Preventive immunotherapy is started early and continued long term because relapses accumulate irreversible deficit; approved biologics target complement, the interleukin-6 receptor or CD19/CD20 B cells.
Other syndromes include brainstem, diencephalic and symptomatic narcolepsy-like presentations reflecting the periventricular distribution of aquaporin-4.
reference.pathophysiology: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is an autoimmune astrocytopathy in which pathogenic immunoglobulin G autoantibodies bind aquaporin-4, the dominant water channel densely expressed on astrocytic foot processes at the blood-brain barrier, in the periependymal regions, optic nerves and spinal cord grey matter. Antibody binding activates the classical complement cascade, producing astrocyte injury and deposition of complement products, followed by an inflammatory infiltrate rich in neutrophils, eosinophils and macrophages that secondarily damages oligodendrocytes and neurones and produces the characteristic necrotic, cavitating lesions. The resulting loss of astrocytic support disrupts glutamate handling and water homeostasis, and the predilection of the disease for the optic nerves, area postrema, hypothalamus and central spinal cord mirrors sites of high aquaporin-4 density and relative blood-brain barrier permeability. Unlike multiple sclerosis, demyelination is a downstream consequence rather than the primary event, and the humoral, complement-dependent mechanism explains both the severity of attacks and the rationale for complement-directed and B-cell-directed therapies. A minority of patients are AQP4-seronegative, and interleukin-6 signalling is implicated in plasmablast survival and antibody production, underpinning interleukin-6 receptor blockade as a treatment strategy.
additionalDifferentials: Spinal cord infarction or dural arteriovenous fistula
Systemic lupus erythematosus or Sjogren-associated myelopathy
Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Serum AQP4-IgG by cell-based assay (preferred over tissue-based or ELISA methods)
Serum MOG-IgG cell-based assay in AQP4-seronegative cases
MRI of the spine showing a longitudinally extensive central cord lesion
MRI brain and orbits with attention to periependymal, area postrema and optic nerve lesions
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis (often pleocytosis with neutrophils; oligoclonal bands usually absent)
Optical coherence tomography and visual evoked potentials to quantify optic nerve involvement
Screening for coexisting autoimmune disease including antinuclear and anti-Ro/anti-La antibodies
redFlags: Rapidly progressive visual loss, particularly if bilateral or with poor initial acuity
Ascending sensorimotor level with sphincter involvement suggesting extensive myelitis
Respiratory compromise from a high cervical or brainstem lesion
Intractable hiccups or vomiting heralding an area postrema attack
Reduced conscious level or autonomic instability from diencephalic or brainstem disease
reference.prognosis: The disorder is typically relapsing and each attack risks permanent visual loss or paraplegia, so untreated disease carries a poor outlook, but early sustained immunotherapy with modern biologics substantially reduces relapse frequency and disability accrual. Prognosis depends heavily on prompt attack treatment and adherence to long-term prevention.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the disorder as multiple sclerosis and starting agents that provoke severe relapses
Relying on oligoclonal bands, which are usually negative and do not exclude the diagnosis
Assuming a single negative AQP4 assay excludes disease; repeat testing and MOG testing may be needed
Underestimating attack severity and delaying escalation to plasma exchange when steroids fail
Overlooking area postrema syndrome and attributing intractable vomiting to a gastrointestinal cause
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
International consensus diagnostic criteria for neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders
Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Treat acute relapses urgently with high-dose intravenous corticosteroids, escalating early to plasma exchange for severe or steroid-unresponsive attacks
Establish long-term relapse prevention with an approved biologic such as eculizumab (complement), satralizumab (interleukin-6 receptor) or inebilizumab (CD19), or with rituximab
Use azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil under corticosteroid cover as maintenance where monoclonal therapies are not accessible
Avoid multiple sclerosis disease-modifying agents such as interferon-beta, natalizumab and fingolimod, which can precipitate deterioration
Confirm the diagnosis by serum AQP4-IgG cell-based assay, testing for MOG-IgG in seronegative cases, to direct appropriate immunotherapy
Provide symptomatic and rehabilitative care for visual impairment, paraplegia, neuropathic pain, spasticity and bladder dysfunction, and manage area postrema symptoms
Coordinate long-term care through a specialist neuro-immunology multidisciplinary team with monitoring for relapse and immunosuppression-related infection
